enrichment.short_title: VAT recovery time bar and ECJ preliminary rulings as facts
key_facts: DFS Furniture Company plc received £13.1m VAT repayment plus £1.5m interest in 1996 after voluntary disclosures, following the Court of Appeal decision in Primback favouring the taxpayer.
The House of Lords referred questions to the ECJ; its 15 May 2001 preliminary ruling supported the Commissioners, and the Lords restored May J's assessment on 11 October 2001.

The Commissioners issued recovery assessments on 24 September and 7 December 2001 under sections 80(4A) and 78A; the VAT Tribunal held the two-year time bar in section 78A(2) had expired because the ECJ judgment was law, not evidence of facts.
The Vice-Chancellor held that the existence, contents and effect of a court judgment are facts or evidence of facts for the purposes of the section 78A(2) time limit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Vice-Chancellor from the VAT and Duties Tribunal on the construction of the section 78A(2) assessment time bar.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Tribunal's decision was set aside.
enrichment.ratio: For the purposes of the two-year time bar in section 78A(2) VAT Act 1994, the existence, contents and effect of a subsequent court judgment—including a preliminary ruling of the European Court of Justice—are facts or evidence of facts capable of starting the limitation period, even though the judgment may also be evidence of the law; excluding such judgments would frustrate the purpose of section 80(4B)(a) and leave taxpayers unable to close their books.
legal_issues: Whether an ECJ preliminary ruling is a fact or evidence of facts for section 78A(2)
Construction of section 80(4A) recovery assessments for overpaid VAT
Interaction between time bars in sections 73(6), 75(2)(b), 77(2A) and 78A(2)
Distinction between a judgment as law and as fact following R v Governor of Brockhill Prison, ex parte Evans (No 2)
linked_authorities: R v Governor of Brockhill Prison, ex parte Evans (No 2)
Pegasus Birds v Commissioners for Customs & Excise
Parekh v Commissioners of Customs & Excise

confidence.notes: Statutory issue, facts and outcome are clearly resolved in the judgment; ratio is explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Planning inquiry fairness and site-visit findings

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning Appeals (Determination by Inspectors) (Inquiries Procedure) (England) Rules 2000

key_facts: Edward Ware New Homes Ltd appealed against refusal of planning permission for ten dwellings with integrated office space on former mushroom-farm buildings at Gatcombe Farm in the Bristol and Bath Green Belt.

A statement of common ground agreed that low-grade employment uses were continuing on site, but paragraph 2.4.3 was deleted just before the inquiry; the Inspector later relied heavily on his site visit to find significant reoccupation unlikely.
The Inspector dismissed the appeal on employment, sustainable development and Green Belt grounds; the Administrative Court dismissed the judicial review.
The Court of Appeal held the Inspector procedurally unfair in not notifying parties under Rule 18(3) before relying on site-visit impressions contrary to the parties' cases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of a section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 application to quash a Planning Inspector's decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Inspector's decision was quashed and the matter remitted to the Secretary of State.
enrichment.ratio: Where an Inspector, after a planning inquiry conducted on the basis of an agreed statement of common ground, forms a materially new view of future fallback use from his own site visit, procedural fairness and Rule 18(3) of the Inquiries Procedure Rules require that he notify the parties and afford them an opportunity to comment before deciding; failure to do so vitiates the decision even if some evidence could support the Inspector's conclusion.
legal_issues: Procedural fairness at planning inquiries
Application of Rule 18(3) to post-inquiry site-visit findings
Weight of Inspector's own observations versus expert evidence
Very special circumstances in the Green Belt
Effect of fall-back employment use on traffic and sustainability assessments
linked_authorities: Fairmount Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment
Wigan NBC v Secretary of State for the Environment
Castleford Homes v Secretary of State for the Environment

confidence.notes: Ground 2 procedural unfairness is the decisive ratio; outcome and facts are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Bail after custody time limit and section 25

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994
Prosecution of Offences (Custody Time Limits) Regulations 1987

key_facts: O faced rape, false imprisonment and indecent assault charges; he had a previous rape conviction, so section 25 Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 applied and bail required exceptional circumstances.
After the custody time limit expired, Judge Sanders refused bail on 9 December 2002; O sought judicial review and habeas corpus.

The Divisional Court held section 29(3) Senior Courts Act 1981 did not bar review because section 22(13) Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 treats custody time limit jurisdiction as non-trial jurisdiction.

Kennedy LJ held amended Regulation 6(6) preserved section 25 after expiry of the custody time limit; Hooper J agreed on dismissal but differed on whether section 25 imposed a legal burden on the defendant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court claim for judicial review and habeas corpus of the Crown Court's refusal to grant bail after expiry of the custody time limit.
enrichment.ratio: Judicial review and habeas corpus are not excluded by section 29(3) Senior Courts Act 1981 in challenges to post-custody-time-limit bail refusals, because section 22(13) Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 treats custody time limit powers as jurisdiction other than trial on indictment; once the custody time limit has expired, amended Regulation 6(6) of the 1987 Regulations does not require unconditional bail where section 25 applies, and a Crown Court judge may lawfully refuse bail if no exceptional circumstances are shown having regard to the gravity of the charge and the defendant's record.
legal_issues: Whether section 29(3) bars review of Crown Court bail decisions after custody time limit expiry
Effect of amended Regulation 6(6) when read with Regulation 5(6B)
Continued application of section 25 after custody time limit expiry
Meaning of satisfied and allocation of burden under section 25
Compatibility of section 25 with Article 5(3) ECHR
Relationship between custody time limit extensions and Article 5(3) reasonableness
index_terms: R v Governor of Canterbury Prison ex parte Craig
linked_authorities: R v Manchester Crown Court ex parte McDonald
R v Governor of Canterbury Prison ex parte Craig

confidence.notes: Outcome and main ratio on jurisdiction and post-CTL bail are clear from Kennedy LJ; Hooper J's split on section 25 burden of proof does not affect dismissal but may warrant citation care.

enrichment.short_title: Palmar arch disease caused by vibratory tools
key_facts: Mr Griggs, a distribution fitter employed by Transco from 1974 to 1998, developed palmar arch disease (PAD) after prolonged use of vibratory tools; the employer admitted breach of duty.

Medical experts agreed PAD affected blood flow through the palmar arch but disputed whether vibration caused it; vascular surgeon Mr Cross attributed it to vibration on a balance-of-probabilities basis, occupational physician Dr Cooke was sceptical.
The county court judge found PAD was vibration-induced and that negligent exposure materially increased the risk; judgment was entered for £211,149.
The Court of Appeal upheld both medical and legal causation, applying McGhee and Fairchild principles to the employer's admitted systemic failures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court personal injury judgment.
enrichment.ratio: On the balance of probabilities a trial judge may find palmar arch disease caused by long-term vibratory tool exposure where alternative causes are excluded and a vascular mechanism is established, even without epidemiological proof in the literature; once medical causation and admitted breaches of duty as to vibration monitoring are proved, legal causation may be satisfied either on a but-for basis or by material increase in risk under McGhee and Fairchild.
legal_issues: Medical causation of palmar arch disease from hand-arm vibration
Diagnosis by exclusion in occupational disease claims
Distinction between HAVS, VWF, PAD and hypothenar hammer syndrome
Legal causation and material increase in risk after Fairchild
Whether negligent versus non-negligent exposure can be distinguished
linked_authorities: Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd
Allen v British Rail Engineering Ltd
Rhesa Shipping SA v Edmunds (The Popi M)

confidence.notes: Medical and legal causation reasoning and dismissal of appeal are fully articulated by Hale LJ.

enrichment.short_title: Straight bill of lading and Hague-Visby Rules

statutes_considered.title: International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law Relating to Bills of Lading (Hague Rules)
Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1971
Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1992

key_facts: MacWilliam purchased printing machinery cif Boston; MSC carried goods from Durban via Felixstowe to Boston on The Rosemary and The Rafaela S under a straight bill of lading naming MacWilliam as consignee.

Goods were badly damaged on the Felixstowe-to-Boston leg; MacWilliam claimed under the Hague-Visby Rules, arguing the straight bill was a bill of lading or similar document of title because surrender was required for delivery.
Langley J and the arbitrators held the straight bill fell outside the Rules; a second issue concerned whether transshipment at Felixstowe created separate contracts.
The Court of Appeal held the straight bill was covered by the Rules where its attestation clause required production for delivery.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from arbitration/Langley J on carriage of goods by sea and application of the Hague-Visby Rules.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the straight bill of lading issue; remaining questions adjourned by agreement.
enrichment.ratio: A straight bill of lading consigned to a named consignee is a bill of lading or similar document of title within Article I(b) of the Hague-Visby Rules where, as in classic bill forms, surrender of an original is required to obtain delivery; negotiability is not an essential characteristic of a bill of lading for Convention purposes, and a document requiring production to obtain possession is a document of title.
legal_issues: Whether a straight bill of lading falls within Hague-Visby Rules Article I(b)
Meaning of similar document of title
Effect of attestation clause requiring surrender of original bills
Distinction between straight bills, order bills and sea waybills
Whether transshipment at Felixstowe created one or two contracts of carriage

confidence.notes: Primary ratio on straight bills is clearly stated; transshipment/contract issue was not finally determined on this appeal.

enrichment.short_title: CCRC murder appeal and trial representation
key_facts: Mark Day was convicted of murder in March 1993 for involvement in a Kingston-upon-Thames street fight in which Mario Commatteo was killed; an earlier appeal was dismissed in 1994.
The CCRC referred the case alleging deficient pre-trial preparation by solicitors and tactical errors by leading counsel, particularly failure to cross-examine co-accused Monaghan.
Prosecution evidence included Miss Tuckwell identifying Day at the fatal attack and palm prints of Day and Steer on a shop window near the scene.

The Court of Appeal found inadequate statement-taking but held no identifiable trial irregularity rendered the conviction unsafe; tactical decisions not to cross-examine Monaghan or call Day were justified.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder conviction following CCRC reference under the Criminal Appeal Act 1995.
enrichment.ratio: Incompetent legal representation does not of itself make a conviction unsafe; the appellant must show that identifiable errors or irregularities at trial rendered the process unfair or unsafe. Where the jury could properly convict on the evidence of an impressive witness corroborated by palm prints, tactical decisions not to cross-examine a co-accused or put the defendant in the witness box do not undermine safety if they were reasonable forensic choices.
legal_issues: Scope of appeals following CCRC references under section 14(5)
When deficient legal representation renders a conviction unsafe
Admissibility and use of co-accused evidence at joint trial
Explanation of palm print evidence
Joint enterprise and separate fights involving Chapman and French

confidence.notes: Outcome and safety test are explicit; fact-intensive representation findings are lengthy but conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt equestrian centre very special circumstances
key_facts: Samuel Smith Old Brewery challenged Selby District Council's September 2002 permission to retain an equestrian centre building in the Green Belt near Tadcaster for Mr and Mrs Hutchinson.
Earlier permissions had failed on highway grounds in 1991-92; PPG2 was revised in 1995, removing the 1988 phrase allowing uses appropriate to a rural area.
The planning officer treated personal circumstances and the pre-1995 highway-only refusals as very special circumstances; modest business profits of £18,000-£27,000 were disclosed.
The court quashed the permission for misdirection on very special circumstances and failure to assess non-visual harm to Green Belt openness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review to quash planning permission for inappropriate Green Belt development.
enrichment.ratio: Personal circumstances and a desire to expand a moderately profitable business cannot without evidence of hardship, unmet need or exhaustive search for alternative sites constitute very special circumstances outweighing harm from inappropriate Green Belt development; a planning authority must treat inappropriate development as harmful by definition and assess loss of openness and impact on Green Belt functions, not merely visual impact.
legal_issues: Very special circumstances under PPG2 paragraph 3.2
Effect of 1995 PPG2 change on reliance on pre-1995 highway-only refusals
Whether personal circumstances can amount to very special circumstances without being relied on by applicants
Assessment of harm to Green Belt openness beyond visual impact
Wednesbury irrationality in planning decisions

linked_authorities: Samuel Smith Old Brewery (Tadcaster) v Selby District Council (Harrison J)

confidence.notes: Two clear grounds of challenge and quashing order are fully reasoned.

key_facts: Lithuanian Roma claimant Mr Bagdanavicius and his wife claimed asylum in December 2002 alleging ill-treatment by the wife's brother and associates, discrimination, and inadequate police protection.
The Secretary of State refused asylum and certified the claim clearly unfounded under section 115, denying an in-country appeal because Lithuania is a listed safe state.
Expert Dr Galeotti's reports on organised crime and anti-Roma prejudice were initially dismissed but later reasoned against on reconsideration.
Maurice Kay J held the claims clearly unfounded: factual account was inconsistent and implausible, internal relocation was available, and sufficiency of protection followed Horvath.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a section 115 Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 clearly unfounded certificate; first substantive judicial scrutiny of the provision.
enrichment.ratio: A section 115 clearly unfounded certificate is justified where, applying the Horvath test of state willingness and ability to provide reasonable protection, no legitimate view of the facts or law could allow the asylum and human rights claims to succeed; the court may reapply the objective test on judicial review, and expert country evidence does not assist where the individual account is inconsistent and internal relocation remains open.
legal_issues: Construction of section 115 clearly unfounded certification
Relationship between section 115(1) and section 115(6)-(7) listed states
Sufficiency of state protection after Horvath v SSHD
Treatment of expert evidence in certification decisions
Internal relocation in Lithuania
Article 3 and Article 8 thresholds for Roma discrimination claims

confidence.notes: First section 115 ruling with detailed reasoning; leave to appeal granted only on sufficiency of protection law.

enrichment.short_title: Moreton Centre care home closure challenge

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: East Sussex County Council decided on 18 December 2002 to close the Moreton Centre residential and day care home in St Leonards-on-Sea and relocate residents by end March 2003.
A £1 million Department of Health grant had been secured to convert the site into a 30-place intermediate care scheme.
Consultation ran from October to November 2002 with individual assessments; claimants challenged consultation, rationality and human rights compliance.
Maurice Kay J dismissed all grounds, finding consultation fair, closure rational given resource constraints, and Articles 2, 3 and 8 not violated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated applications for judicial review of a local authority decision to close a council-owned residential care home.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority may lawfully decide to close a residential care home after fair consultation where individual assessments have been carried out, alternative provision exists, and closure is justified by value-for-money review and securing central government funding; closure decisions involving relocation of elderly residents do not breach Article 8 where justified for economic well-being and resource allocation, and do not reach Article 3 severity merely because transfer carries managed mortality risk.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of consultation under ex parte Coughlan principles
Wednesbury rationality and consideration of mortality research on home transfers
Relevance of the Cowl report guidelines
Application of Articles 2, 3 and 8 ECHR to care home closure
Whether alternative placements must be identified before closure decision

R v Plymouth City Council ex parte Cowl

confidence.notes: Three grounds comprehensively addressed with clear dismissal on each.

key_facts: Paul Ali Hayter was convicted of murder as alleged middleman in a contract killing of Mario Commatteo procured by Angela Bristow and carried out by Ryan.

Ryan's guilt depended on out-of-court admissions to his girlfriend; Bristow's role was proved circumstantially; Hayter's case was entirely circumstantial and depended on proving Ryan was the killer and Bristow the procurer.
Hayter argued there was no case to answer because Ryan's inadmissible confessions could not prove a fact essential to convicting Hayter.
The Court of Appeal held a jury satisfied of Ryan's guilt on evidence admissible against Ryan may use that established fact against Hayter; section 74(1) PACE undermines Spinks and Rhodes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder conviction with leave of the Full Court on whether the trial judge erred in ruling there was a case to answer.
enrichment.ratio: Where proof of another person's guilt is a legal precondition to convicting the defendant, a jury in a joint trial may rely on a conclusion reached on evidence admissible against that co-accused even though the same evidence would be inadmissible against the defendant directly; following section 74(1) PACE 1984, Spinks and Rhodes no longer support excluding such use, because a prior conviction would now be admissible to prove the underlying offence in separate proceedings.
legal_issues: Use of co-accused out-of-court admissions to prove facts against another defendant
Whether there is a case to answer where secondary liability depends on principal's guilt
Effect of section 74(1) PACE on Spinks, Rhodes and Hickey
Joint trial versus separate trial evidential rules
Middleman liability in murder and section 4 Criminal Law Act 1967
linked_authorities: Hollington v F Hewthorn & Co Ltd

confidence.notes: Single ground of appeal concisely resolved with explicit departure from pre-PACE authority.
